title: Heating and cooling — specific heat capacity explained
examTip: ΔE = mcΔθ. Remember: Δ means 'change in'. Δθ is the temperature CHANGE (final − initial), not the final temperature.
introTips: Water takes a long time to heat up and cool down. This is specific heat capacity in action.
Δθ means change in temperature. If water goes from 20°C to 100°C, Δθ = 80°C.
Different materials need very different amounts of energy to change temperature by the same amount.
intro: The sea stays warm long after summer ends, keeping coastal towns milder than inland cities. Why? The answer is specific heat capacity. It is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. It is why water is used in car radiators and central heating. It is why coastal climates are gentler. It is also why a pie filling can burn your mouth while the pastry feels fine. This is one of the most important (and most examined) equations in physics.

keyPoints.heading: Specific heat capacity
keyPoints.content: Heating increases the energy of the particles in a system. This either raises the temperature or changes the state. If the temperature rises, the rise depends on three things. These are the mass of the substance, the type of material and the energy put in. Different materials need different amounts of energy to change their temperature by the same amount. Specific heat capacity has the symbol c. It is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. Units: J/kg°C. The equation is: ΔE = mcΔθ Change in thermal energy (J) = mass (kg) × specific heat capacity (J/kg°C) × change in temperature (°C). Water has an unusually high specific heat capacity = 4200 J/kg°C. It takes a lot of energy to heat it up. It releases a lot of energy as it cools down. This is why water is used as a coolant in car radiators. It is also used as a store of thermal energy in central heating. It takes in and releases large amounts of energy without big swings in temperature.
writeBullets: Specific heat capacity (c) — energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. Unit: J/kg°C
ΔE = mcΔθ — change in thermal energy (J) = mass (kg) × specific heat capacity (J/kg°C) × temperature change (°C)
Δθ — change in temperature = final temperature − initial temperature
Water specific heat capacity = 4200 J/kg°C. Very high: it takes a lot of energy to heat up and cools slowly
High specific heat capacity = good store of thermal energy. Used in central heating, car cooling and keeping coastal climates steady

keyTerms.def: The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C; unit: J/kg°C
Change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
Change in temperature (°C) = final temperature − initial temperature

keyPoints.memTip: ΔE = mcΔθ. Say it as 'em-see-delta-theta'. m = mass, c = specific heat capacity, Δθ = temp change.
keyPoints.tutor_note: A common mistake is using the final temperature instead of the temperature change. Every time, Δθ = final temperature − initial temperature.

keyPoints.heading: Using ΔE = mcΔθ
keyPoints.content: The equation ΔE = mcΔθ can be rearranged to find any variable. Rearrangements: m = ΔE / (cΔθ), c = ΔE / (mΔθ), Δθ = ΔE / (mc). Worked example 1: how much energy is needed to heat 2 kg of water from 20°C to 100°C? Δθ = 80°C. ΔE = 2 × 4200 × 80 = 672,000 J = 672 kJ. Worked example 2: a 1.5 kg block of aluminium (c = 900 J/kg°C) cools from 80°C to 20°C. Energy is released as it cools. Use the size of the temperature change, 60°C. Energy released = 1.5 × 900 × 60 = 81,000 J = 81 kJ. Worked example 3: 5 kg of a material takes in 15,000 J. Its temperature rises by 10°C. What is its specific heat capacity? c = ΔE / (mΔθ) = 15,000 / (5 × 10) = 300 J/kg°C.
writeBullets: ΔE = mcΔθ — the standard form. Use it to work out energy transferred
c = ΔE / (mΔθ) — rearranged to find specific heat capacity
m = ΔE / (cΔθ) — rearranged to find mass
Δθ = ΔE / (mc) — rearranged to find temperature change
Example: 2 kg water, 20°C to 100°C → ΔE = 2 × 4200 × 80 = 672,000 J

keyTerms.def: c = ΔE/(mΔθ); m = ΔE/(cΔθ); Δθ = ΔE/(mc)

keyPoints.memTip: To find c: c = ΔE divided by (m times Δθ). Write the rearrangement before substituting numbers.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Worked examples 2 and 3 are common exam question styles. One is cooling (energy released). The other is finding an unknown specific heat capacity. Practise all three types.

keyPoints.heading: Required practical — measuring specific heat capacity
keyPoints.content: This is a required practical. Expect questions about the method, sources of error and how to improve accuracy. The practical links a decrease in one energy store (or work done) to a rise in temperature. That rise shows an increase in thermal energy stored. Method: heat a known mass (m) of a substance with an electrical heater. The substance is water or a metal block. Measure the energy supplied with a joulemeter. Or find the power using P = IV (current × potential difference). Then use E = Pt. Measure the temperature change (Δθ) with a thermometer. Calculate c = ΔE / (mΔθ). For a metal block: the heater fits into a hole in the block. A thermometer sits in a second hole. For water: heat it in a polystyrene cup. Stir all the time so the temperature is even. Sources of error: - heat loss to the surroundings (less energy went into the substance than you think) - not all the work done by the heater heats the substance (some heats the heater itself) - reading the thermometer before the temperature has settled Improvements: wrap the block or container in insulation to reduce heat loss. Stir water so the temperature is even all through. Wait for the temperature to settle before recording.
writeBullets: Method: heat a known mass with an electrical heater. Measure the energy supplied and Δθ. Calculate c = ΔE/(mΔθ)
Joulemeter — a device that measures electrical energy directly in joules
Energy supplied — from a joulemeter, or from P = IV and then E = Pt
Error: some energy is lost to the surroundings. So the energy supplied is more than the sample received. This makes the calculated c too high
Error: the heater also heats itself, not just the sample. This overestimates the energy input
Improvement: insulate the sample well. Stir water. Wait for the temperature to settle before reading

keyTerms.def: An instrument that directly measures electrical energy in joules

keyPoints.memTip: For the practical: measure the energy supplied. Then c = ΔE/(mΔθ). Remember to insulate to reduce heat loss error.
keyPoints.tutor_note: This practical almost always comes up in the exam. Be able to describe the method and name two sources of error. Suggest improvements, with scientific reasons.

keyPoints.heading: Thermal stores and temperature
keyPoints.content: Thermal energy is stored in the internal energy of a system. Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles that make up a system. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. The hotter the substance, the faster its particles move on average. This matters. Temperature measures the average KE per particle. Internal energy depends on temperature AND the number of particles. Energy is transferred by heating from a hotter object to a cooler one. Uses of high specific heat capacity: - water in central heating carries a lot of energy per kg - coastal climates are milder than inland areas. The sea's high specific heat capacity evens out temperature changes. It warms up and cools down slowly - solar thermal panels use water to store energy collected from sunlight
writeBullets: Internal energy — the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles that make up a system
Temperature — a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles. Higher temp = faster particles
Energy is transferred by heating from a hotter object to a cooler one
Uses of high specific heat capacity: central heating water, steadier coastal climates, solar thermal panels

keyTerms.def: The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles that make up a system
How hot or cold something is, measured in °C. It is related to the average kinetic energy of the particles

keyPoints.memTip: Temperature = average KE per particle. Internal energy = total energy of ALL particles.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Temperature and internal energy are easy to mix up. A large cold lake has more internal energy than a tiny hot spark. That is true even though the spark is at a higher temperature.

tables.title: Specific heat capacities of common materials

0.question: How much energy is needed to heat 3 kg of water (c = 4200 J/kg°C) from 15°C to 65°C?
0.wrongFeedback: Use ΔE = mcΔθ. First find Δθ = 65 − 15 = 50°C. Then ΔE = 3 × 4200 × 50 = 630,000 J. Remember: Δθ is the CHANGE in temperature, not the final temperature.

1.question: A 2 kg block of aluminium (c = 900 J/kg°C) cools from 70°C to 20°C. How much energy does it release?
1.correctFeedback: Correct! The size of the temperature change is 70 − 20 = 50°C. ΔE = 2 × 900 × 50 = 90,000 J = 90 kJ.
1.wrongFeedback: Use ΔE = mcΔθ with the size of the temperature change. Δθ = 70 − 20 = 50°C. ΔE = 2 × 900 × 50 = 90,000 J.

2.question: In the specific heat capacity required practical, why is insulation put around the metal block?
options: To reduce energy transfer to the surroundings. So more of the energy supplied goes into the block
To speed up the rate at which the block heats up
To prevent the thermometer from touching the block directly
To increase the specific heat capacity of the block
2.correctFeedback: Exactly right! Insulation reduces energy transfer to the surroundings. So more of the measured energy supplied goes into the block. The calculated specific heat capacity is then more accurate.
2.wrongFeedback: Insulation reduces heat loss to the surroundings. Without it, some of the energy supplied heats the air around the block instead of the block. That makes the calculated specific heat capacity bigger than the true value.

3.question: A large lake is cold. A small spark is very hot. Which statement is correct?
options: The lake can have more internal energy, even though the spark is at a higher temperature
The spark must have more internal energy, because it is hotter
They must have the same internal energy
Temperature and internal energy are the same thing
3.correctFeedback: Correct! Internal energy is the total energy of all the particles. The lake has a huge number of particles, so it can have more internal energy.
3.wrongFeedback: Temperature is linked to the average kinetic energy of the particles. Internal energy is the total energy of all the particles. A large lake has so many particles that it can have more internal energy than a hot spark.

commonMistakes: Using the final temperature instead of the temperature change in ΔE = mcΔθ. Always work out Δθ = final temperature − initial temperature first.
Forgetting to convert mass to kg. If mass is given in grams, divide by 1000 before substituting.
Mixing up temperature (average KE of particles) and internal energy (total energy of all particles). They are different quantities.
In the required practical, naming heat loss as an error without saying its effect. Say it makes the measured specific heat capacity higher than the true value.
Thinking a higher temperature always means more internal energy. A large cold object can have more internal energy than a small hot one.
examTips: ΔE = mcΔθ. Always find Δθ (the change in temperature) first. Write it out before substituting. If an object cools, energy is released. Use the size of the temperature change for Δθ.
The required practical has two main sources of error. (1) Heat loss to the surroundings. (2) The heater also heats itself. Both make the calculated specific heat capacity too high.
Uses of high specific heat capacity are common 2–3 mark questions. Clearly link water's high specific heat capacity to central heating, coastal climates or solar thermal systems.
To work out specific heat capacity from experimental data, use c = ΔE/(mΔθ). Then discuss why your answer may differ from the true value (systematic errors).
